title: Basic Calculator II
description: Brute force to optimized: a general two-stack precedence-climbing parser versus a simpler single-stack technique tracking only the previous operator.

blocks.text: Given a string s representing a basic (parenthesis-free) arithmetic expression, containing non-negative integers and the operators +, -, *, and / (with standard operator precedence: * and / before + and -), evaluate the expression and return its value. Integer division truncates toward zero. The expression may contain spaces.

blocks.caption: "+" and "-" defer their signed value onto a stack; "*" and "/" resolve immediately against the stack's current top, since they have higher precedence

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A string s representing a valid arithmetic expression"],["Output","The integer result of evaluating the expression, respecting standard operator precedence"],["Goal","Correctly apply * and / BEFORE + and -, in a single linear pass, without building a full parse tree"],["Constraints","1 <= s.length <= 3*10^5; s consists of digits, ' ', '+', '-', '*', '/'; the expression is valid and evaluates to an integer in the 32-bit range"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Operator PRECEDENCE must be respected (* and / bind tighter than + and -)","A stack naturally defers lower-precedence operations while immediately resolving higher-precedence ones as soon as they are seen"],["No parentheses are involved (simplifying the grammar)","A single left-to-right pass suffices, tracking only the PREVIOUS operator, rather than needing a full recursive-descent parser"]]}

blocks.text: Unlike simple left-to-right evaluation, "*" and "/" must be applied BEFORE "+" and "-", regardless of their position in the string; this requires deferring the addition/subtraction terms until it is certain no higher-precedence operation still needs to modify them first.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building a Grocery Receipt Where Discounts Apply Before the Final Total
blocks.text: Imagine tallying a grocery receipt where each item's price might first need a multiplier or division applied (like a "buy 2 get discount" multiplier) before it becomes a fixed LINE ITEM that simply gets added to (or subtracted from) the final total. Each line item, once its own multiplication/division is fully resolved, is placed onto a running list of "final, signed line items"; the grand total is just the sum of that list at the very end.

blocks.caption: "+" and "-" push a new signed line item onto the stack; "*" and "/" instead modify the MOST RECENT line item in place, since they bind more tightly

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Stack after","Why"],"rows":[["Parse \"3\", see \"+\": push 3","[3]","A pending \"+\" simply defers the number as a new signed term"],["Parse \"5\", see \"/\": push 5, then immediately resolve using the operator BEFORE this new number (still \"+\")... actually: push 5 first (op was \"+\"), THEN \"/\", applied to the NEXT number","[3,5]","The \"/\" seen here applies to the upcoming number (2), not to 5 directly"],["Parse \"2\", end of string (flushed): op is \"/\", so pop 5, compute 5/2=2 (truncated), push 2","[3,2]","\"/\" resolves immediately against the most recent pushed term"],["Answer","sum([3,2]) = 5","Matches the expected result"]]}

blocks.text: Before building an explicit expression tree or fully parsing operator precedence recursively, notice that tracking just the PREVIOUS operator, combined with a stack of already-resolved signed terms, is enough to correctly apply precedence in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A number is always associated with the operator that immediately PRECEDED it (or "+" implicitly, for the very first number).

Observation 2: If that preceding operator is "+" or "-", the number (correctly signed) can simply be pushed onto the stack as a new, independent term, since addition and subtraction do not need to "look ahead" at what comes next.

Observation 3: If the preceding operator is "*" or "/", the number must instead be combined IMMEDIATELY with whatever is currently on TOP of the stack (popping it, computing the result, and pushing the combined value back), since multiplication and division bind more tightly and must be resolved before any later addition/subtraction can safely proceed.

Observation 4: By the time the entire string (plus a convenient trailing "+" sentinel to flush the final number) has been processed, the stack contains only fully-resolved, independent signed terms; the final answer is simply their sum.

This is a stack-based single-pass technique: "+"/"-" defer a new signed term onto the stack, while "*"/"/" immediately combine with the stack's current top, correctly respecting operator precedence without any explicit parsing structure.

Use a general-purpose two-stack (numbers and operators) shunting-yard-style approach, explicitly comparing operator precedence and resolving pending operators whenever a new one of equal or lower precedence arrives.

items: Parse numbers and operators from the string; push numbers onto a number stack.
Before pushing a new operator, repeatedly resolve any pending operator on the operator stack that has precedence >= the new one's (applying it to the top two numbers), then push the new operator.
After the full string is processed, resolve any remaining pending operators to get the final answer.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: This is a general precedence-climbing technique (similar to the Shunting Yard algorithm), correctly handling operator precedence for ANY set of operators, not just this specific problem's four.
It works correctly, but is more general (and slightly more complex) than strictly necessary for a grammar with only two precedence levels.

blocks.text: Correctly evaluates the expression, respecting operator precedence, since it explicitly compares precedence levels before resolving any pending operator.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass, since each number and operator is processed a constant number of times.
Space: O(n), for the two stacks in the worst case.

Limitation: this general two-stack precedence-climbing approach is more machinery than necessary for a grammar with only TWO precedence levels; a simpler single-stack technique (tracking just the previous operator) achieves the identical result with less bookkeeping.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since this specific grammar has only two precedence levels (+/- vs. */), the general operator-stack machinery is unnecessary. Instead, track just ONE variable: the operator that preceded the CURRENT number being parsed. When a new operator (or the end of the string) is reached, use that PRECEDING operator to decide what to do: "+"/"-" push a new signed term; "*"/"/" combine immediately with the stack's current top.

Append a trailing "+" to the (space-stripped) string, ensuring the final number is always flushed identically to every other number. Walk through the string, accumulating digits into num. On any non-digit character: based on the PREVIOUS operator (op), either push num (or -num) onto the stack, or pop the stack's top and combine it with num via multiplication or truncating division, pushing the result back. Update op to the current character, and reset num to 0. Return the sum of the final stack.
Track just the previous operator; "+"/"-" defer a new signed term onto the stack, while "*"/"/" immediately combine with the stack's current top.
Dry run for s = "3+5/2" (with a trailing "+" appended)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (a long chain of + and - terms).

Because "*" and "/" bind more tightly than "+" and "-", a number preceded by "*" or "/" must ALWAYS combine with whatever number came immediately before it (already resolved, sitting on top of the stack), rather than being treated as its own independent term. Deferring "+" and "-" terms onto the stack (rather than immediately summing them) correctly delays their combination until every higher-precedence operation touching them has already been resolved.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Previous operator was \"+\"","The new number is pushed directly onto the stack"],["Previous operator was \"-\"","The NEGATED new number is pushed onto the stack"],["Previous operator was \"*\" or \"/\"","The stack's current top is popped, combined with the new number, and the result is pushed back"]]}

items: Appending a trailing "+" sentinel to the string is a clean trick that avoids needing separate "flush the final number" logic after the main loop.
The op variable always represents "the operator that came BEFORE the number just finished being parsed," which is exactly what determines how that number should be combined.

Truncating division (not floor division) is achieved naturally in Java/C++ via their built-in integer division semantics, while Python requires an explicit int() cast after true division to achieve the same truncation-toward-zero behavior.

blocks.text: When a grammar has a SMALL, FIXED number of precedence levels (here, just two: */  above +/-), a single stack combined with tracking only the immediately preceding operator is sufficient to correctly evaluate the expression in one pass, without needing a full general-purpose precedence-climbing parser.

items: Forgetting to flush the final number (no trailing operator naturally triggers its processing), typically fixed by appending a sentinel operator to the string.
Using floor division instead of truncating-toward-zero division for negative results (e.g., -3 / 2 should give -1, not -2).
Confusing WHICH operator determines an action: it is always the operator that PRECEDED the just-finished number, not the operator currently being read.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single number with no operators","The trailing \"+\" sentinel correctly flushes it as the only stack entry, summing to itself"],["Consecutive spaces or spaces around operators","Stripped entirely before processing, since they carry no semantic meaning here"],["A chain of only \"*\" and \"/\" (e.g., \"2*3/2\")","Each resolves immediately against the running top, correctly producing a single final term"]]}

items: Explicitly stating "since there are only two precedence levels, tracking just the PREVIOUS operator suffices, no general parser needed" demonstrates recognizing the simpler structure this specific problem allows, compared to a fully general expression evaluator.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Evaluate an expression with operator PRECEDENCE, but NO parentheses" points toward a single-stack, track-the-previous-operator technique, simpler than a full precedence-climbing parser.

items: How would you extend this to support parentheses as well? A recursive approach (or an explicit stack of "contexts," pushing a new evaluation frame on "(" and popping/combining on ")") would be needed, closely related to Basic Calculator (the parentheses-supporting variant).

How would you handle unary minus (e.g., "-3+5")? Special-case an operator appearing at the very start (or right after another operator) as applying to a leading implicit 0, or otherwise directly negate the following number.
What is the space complexity in the WORST case, and when does it occur? O(n), when the expression is a long chain of "+" and "-" terms, since each pushes a new, never-combined stack entry.

A simplified, single-stack variant of the general expression-evaluation pattern also used in Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation elsewhere in this category, here additionally handling INFIX notation and operator precedence directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single stack, track previous operator): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Single-stack expression evaluation, tracking only the previous operator
Core Idea: "+"/"-" defer a new signed term onto the stack; "*"/"/" immediately combine with the stack's current top, correctly respecting the grammar's two precedence levels in one linear pass
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: A number's handling is determined by the operator that PRECEDED it, not the operator currently being read
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: "+"/"-" push (signed); "*"/"/" pop-combine-push; sum the final stack
